source: Transverse and Longitudinal Waves
In a transverse wave the medium moves across the wave's path; in a longitudinal wave it moves back and forth along it.
Students think every wave is transverse, like a water wave, and can't picture sound as squeezes and stretches of the air.

Every wave makes the medium move, but not always in the same direction. Shake a rope up and down and the wiggle runs along it. Push and pull the end of a long spring and a squeeze runs along it. Those are the two basic kinds of waves.

In a transverse wave, the medium moves across (perpendicular to) the direction the wave travels: crests and troughs. In a longitudinal wave, the medium moves back and forth along the direction the wave travels: compressions (squeezed) and rarefactions (spread out). Sound is longitudinal.

A loudspeaker cone pushes forward, squeezing the air in front of it, then pulls back, leaving the air spread out. Those squeezes and stretches travel outward, while each bit of air just jiggles back and forth along the wave's path. The distance from one compression to the next is the wavelength, just as crest to crest is for a transverse wave.
A longitudinal wave, slowed down: particles crowd together and spread apart. Each one moves only left and right around its own spot.
A stadium crowd does "the wave": each person stands up and sits down as the wave sweeps around the stadium. Which kind of wave is it?
Classify the wave
Transverse
Each person moves up and down.
The wave travels sideways around the stadium.
Motion across the direction of travel: transverse.
In a sound wave, the compressions are 1.2 m apart. What is the wavelength?
Wavelength of sound
One compression to the next is one full wave.
So $\lambda = 1.2$ m. (Compression to the next rarefaction would be only half a wave.)

Thinking every wave is transverse, like the picture of a water wave, and being unable to picture sound. Sound has no crests in the air; it is a train of squeezes and stretches moving outward. (Water waves are actually a mix: the water at the surface moves in small circles.)

Earthquakes send both kinds. Longitudinal P waves travel fastest and arrive first; transverse S waves arrive later and cannot cross Earth's liquid outer core, which is one of the ways scientists learned the outer core is liquid.
